title: CuTe DSL Calling Conventions Overview
key_concepts: Execution contexts: Python, Host JIT, Device
critical_patterns: Python → @cute.jit: Entry point for JIT-compiled functions
constraints: Static arguments must be known at compile time
Dynamic arguments are passed at runtime
Tensors are passed by reference, not copied
compressed_summary: CuTe DSL's calling conventions are essential for building efficient GPU programs. The key principle is distinguishing between compile-time (inlined) and runtime (dynamic GPU launch) calls. There are three execution contexts: Python (CPU, dynamic), Host JIT (@cute.jit, CPU, orchestrates GPU work), and Device (@cute.kernel, GPU, parallel execution). Python can call @cute.jit functions directly but must use .launch() from @cute.jit to invoke @cute.kernel functions. JIT functions can call other JIT functions and Python functions, with the former being inlined for optimization. Kernels cannot dynamically call other kernels due to the lack of support for CUDA Dynamic Parallelism. Argument passing is divided into static (compile-time known) and dynamic (runtime known), with static arguments enabling optimizations like loop unrolling. Tensors are always passed by reference, ensuring no copying overhead. Synchronization between kernel launches is implicit within the same stream, but explicit control can be achieved using CUDA streams. Common patterns include multi-kernel pipelines, conditional kernel selection, and iterative kernel calls. Performance considerations highlight the benefits of inlining for zero overhead and the importance of minimizing launch overhead by consolidating kernel operations. Debugging tools include call tracing and compile-time print statements. For further exploration, topics like JIT caching and control flow in different contexts are recommended.
